Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing

How to get and use rough sizes from engineers without quietly converting them into promises you will be held to.

1. Bengaluru, 14 April 2026

Meera Ranganathan had been Director of Product at Patang Money for eleven months, and the meeting she was walking into was the one she had been warned about. Patang is a consumer savings and investment app — about 3.1 million monthly active users, most of them first-time investors putting ₹500 to ₹2,000 a month into mutual funds through UPI. The plan on the table was called Sachet SIP: a product that would let a user commit as little as ₹50 a week through a UPI Autopay mandate, with the amount stepping up automatically as the user's salary credits grew. The growth team had modelled it as the single biggest lever on activation in the festive quarter.

The commercial fact that made the meeting tense was this. Patang's marketing head had already booked ₹4.2 crore of festive media — connected TV, vernacular audio, and a regional cricket property — with the flight starting 12 October 2026, three weeks ahead of Diwali on 8 November. The inventory was paid for. It could not be moved. If Sachet SIP was not in production and stable by 30 September, Patang would spend ₹4.2 crore driving traffic to a product that did not exist.

Meera had asked Arvind Boruah, the engineering manager for the Autopay pod, for an estimate. What she got back, on a shared document, was a list of nine work items with letters next to them: L, M, M, L, M, S, S, M, XS. No dates. No hours. Arvind's covering note said: "Rough sizes. Don't read them as a plan yet."

The CEO, joining from Singapore, opened the meeting by asking the obvious question: "So can we do it by the end of September or not?" Meera had roughly ninety seconds to decide what kind of answer she was going to give. She could give a date, which would be treated as a commitment by everyone in the room and would bind a team she did not manage. She could refuse to give a date, which would read as evasion and would probably get her overruled. Or she could do something harder: turn nine letters into a defensible statement about likelihood, say out loud what would have to be true, and name the one thing that would move the answer most.

This page is about the third option, and about why the first two are both failures of the same idea.

2. The idea: a size is not a date

An estimate is a prediction of how much work something contains, made under uncertainty, by the people who will do the work. A commitment is a promise to deliver something by a date. A target is a business-desired date, arrived at independently of the work. A forecast is a statement about the probability of a date, derived from estimates plus observed history plus capacity. These four things are routinely collapsed into one number in a slide, and almost every dysfunction in software planning starts with that collapse. Steve McConnell, whose 2006 book Software Estimation: Demystifying the Black Art is the standard reference, makes the distinction the spine of the whole subject: an estimate that has been negotiated is no longer an estimate, because reality does not negotiate.

T-shirt sizing is a deliberately coarse estimation scale — XS, S, M, L, XL — used to size items of work relative to each other rather than in absolute time. It belongs to a family of techniques that emerged from Extreme Programming in the late 1990s. Kent Beck and Ron Jeffries introduced story points around 1997–99 as a unit that was explicitly not hours; James Grenning invented Planning Poker in 2002 to stop the loudest engineer in the room anchoring everyone else, and Mike Cohn popularised it in Agile Estimating and Planning (2005). The deeper ancestor is older: Barry Boehm's Wideband Delphi, described in Software Engineering Economics (1981), itself adapted from the RAND Corporation's Delphi method of the 1950s, in which experts estimate independently, see each other's numbers, discuss the reasons for divergence, and re-estimate.

The problem all of this was invented to solve is specific and worth stating plainly. Software teams are systematically bad at predicting absolute durations, and the badness is not random — it is biased optimistic, because the work you have not yet understood is invisible to you and therefore weighs nothing in your mental model. But teams are considerably better at comparison: at saying "this is about like that one, maybe a bit bigger." Relative sizing exploits the human faculty that works and avoids the one that does not. The letters are then converted into time not by a lookup table someone invented, but by the team's own observed history: how long did the things we called L actually take, last quarter?

"That is a size, not a date. I will give you a date when we have finished the first slice and I can price the rest against it."

That is the sentence Meera can say in a board meeting without sounding evasive, because it contains a commitment — to produce a date, by a named point, from evidence rather than from optimism.

3. How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics are simple to describe and are almost always executed with two or three steps left implicit, which is where the damage happens. Here is the full sequence as Arvind's pod runs it.

Step one: fix a reference item. Relative sizing is meaningless without an anchor. Before sizing anything, the team names one piece of work everyone remembers and agrees it is an M. At Patang the reference M is "add a new failure reason to the mandate error taxonomy, end to end, including the app string and the ops dashboard" — a job the pod did in early February that took a little over a week of one engineer's time. Every other item is then sized by asking "bigger or smaller than that, and by roughly how much?" Teams that skip this step are not doing relative estimation; they are doing absolute estimation with letters on top, and their letters drift in meaning from quarter to quarter.

Step two: size effort, complexity and uncertainty together — not duration. A size answers "how much work is in here, including the work of finding out what the work is," not "how many calendar days will pass." Two items can be the same size and take wildly different amounts of calendar time if one waits three weeks on an external partner. Calendar time is a forecasting problem, handled in step six.

Step three: the people who will do the work do the sizing. Estimates made by an architect who will not write the code, or by a PM who "just wants a ballpark," are not estimates; they are anchors. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman showed in 1974 that an arbitrary number mentioned before a judgement drags the judgement towards it, and the effect survives people knowing about it. The practical rule is that the PM may describe the problem and answer questions, and may not say a number first.

Step four — usually implicit — write down what would make this bigger. For each item, the team records the one or two assumptions that, if false, change the size. This list is worth more than the letters. "L, assuming the AMC partner exposes a REST order API" is a usable estimate. "L" alone is not.

Step five — also implicit — split anything that comes out XL. XL is not a size, it is a signal that the item is not understood well enough to be sized. Relative judgement is reliable within roughly one order of magnitude; beyond that, people are guessing. The correct response to XL is to break the item down or to spend a fixed, timeboxed amount of effort (a spike) buying the information that would let you size it.

Step six: convert to time using observed history, as a range. The pod keeps a record of how long past items of each size actually took, in engineer-days. That distribution — not a conversion constant — is what turns letters into a forecast. And the forecast is stated as a range with a confidence attached, because a single date is a claim about certainty the team does not possess.

Step seven: re-estimate when knowledge arrives, and say so. An estimate has a shelf life. The discipline is to re-run the arithmetic the moment an assumption breaks and to communicate the change immediately — not at the end of the quarter, when it is news instead of information.

4. Nine letters, worked line by line

Here is what Meera actually did between 14 and 17 April. She started not with the nine items but with Patang's own history, because without it the letters convert into nothing. Arvind's pod had completed 41 items over the previous two quarters, and each had carried a size when it started. Meera pulled the engineer-days actually spent on each and looked at the distribution by size.

Anyone who writes "L = 2 × M" in a spreadsheet is inventing arithmetic the data does not support. Second, the spread inside each size is enormous — an L has come in at 19 days and at 51 days. That spread is the estimate's real information content, and it is exactly what a single-number plan throws away.

The composition is two Ls, four Ms, two Ss and one XS. Using the medians from Exhibit 1: (2 × 19) + (4 × 8) + (2 × 3) + (1 × 1) = 38 + 32 + 6 + 1 = 77 engineer-days. Using the 80th percentiles: (2 × 38) + (4 × 15) + (2 × 6) + (1 × 2) = 76 + 60 + 12 + 2 = 150 engineer-days.

A note on that second number, because it is the most commonly abused step in the whole practice. Adding up the 80th percentile of every item does not give the 80th percentile of the total; if item risks were independent it would give something closer to a 95th percentile, because it assumes every item goes badly at once. Here, though, the risks are not independent — seven of the nine items depend on the same sponsor-bank certification — so treating the sum of the p80s as a plausible bad case is defensible. Knowing why you are allowed to do the arithmetic is the difference between estimating and performing estimation.

Against that, capacity. Six engineers, 63 working days in the quarter, is 378 engineer-days gross. Patang's measured focus factor — the share of gross time that has historically gone into planned feature work rather than production support, interviews, leave and festival holidays — is 0.55, giving 208 engineer-days. The pod also owes about 30 engineer-days of committed security remediation. That leaves 178 engineer-days for Sachet SIP.

So: median case 77 days against 178 available, which looks luxurious. Bad case 150 against 178, which fits with 16 percent to spare. On 14 April, the honest reading was "probably yes, and we should still not promise."

The second pass: one input moves

On 22 April the partner AMC's technology team confirmed what Arvind had feared. There was no REST order API. Orders had to go through the registrar's file-based settlement window, with a three-week certification slot that could not be brought forward, and a separate end-of-day reconciliation file format. Item 4 was re-sized from L to XL — which, by the pod's own rule, meant it had to be split — and a new M appeared for file reconciliation.

The composition became one XL, one L, five Ms, two Ss, one XS. Medians: 45 + 19 + (5 × 8) + (2 × 3) + 1 = 111 engineer-days. Eightieth percentiles: 95 + 38 + (5 × 15) + (2 × 6) + 2 = 222 engineer-days.

The median still fits inside capacity at 62 percent. The bad case does not: 222 against 178 is a 25 percent overrun. Meera's statement to the CEO on 24 April was therefore not "yes" and not "no" but this: "At our measured throughput, we finish all nine items by 30 September with roughly 55 to 60 percent confidence. To get above 85 percent we must either drop two items or move the go-live to 21 October. The single biggest lever is the registrar certification slot, and I can buy certainty on that within two weeks."

5. Eight nuances a learner must absorb

Estimate, target, commitment and forecast are four different objects

The festive date of 30 September was a target: it came from media inventory, not from the work. Arvind's letters were estimates. The number Meera gave the CEO was a forecast. A commitment would be a promise to deliver by a date, and the only honest basis for one is a forecast with enough confidence that the promiser is willing to be judged on it. Collapsing the four is how a business target becomes an engineering failure: nobody estimated anything, but somebody will be blamed.

Relative sizing works because comparison is easier than absolute judgement — within limits

People are reliably better at "bigger or smaller than that" than at "how many days." But the reliability holds only over a limited range. Asked to compare something ten times larger than the anchor, judgement degrades sharply. This is why XL is a trigger to split, not a size, and why a scale of five buckets is enough. Adding XXL and XXXL does not add precision; it adds the appearance of precision to a region where none exists.

Sizes are ordinal; only history makes them arithmetical

You cannot add letters. You can add the empirical distributions attached to letters by this team, over a recent window, on comparable work. A size chart borrowed from another team, another product, or last year's staffing is a decoration. If a team has never recorded actuals against sizes, its T-shirt sizes cannot be converted to time at all, and saying so out loud is the correct first move.

The uncertainty lives in the work as well as in the estimate

A frequent misreading of the cone of uncertainty is that estimates get better as people get more experienced. They do, a little. But the dominant effect is that the work itself becomes less uncertain as decisions are made and unknowns are closed. Pressing a team to "just be more accurate" at the wide end of the cone asks them to know something nobody knows. The productive request is different: what is the cheapest thing we could build or learn that would narrow the range?

Whoever speaks first sets the number

Anchoring is not a weakness of junior engineers; it is a property of human judgement. A PM who says "I was thinking this is a two-week job, what do you think?" has not asked a question. The counter-measure is procedural: silent independent estimates first, revealed together, with discussion focused on why the high and low estimators see different work — which is where the real information is. The outlier is usually the only person in the room who has spotted something.

The biggest lever is scope, not estimation accuracy

Meera could have spent three more weeks refining the nine letters and improved her forecast by perhaps ten percent. Dropping the iOS onboarding screens for launch, or shipping reconciliation as a nightly spreadsheet instead of a report, moved the number far more. Estimation exists to inform scope decisions; a team that estimates beautifully and never changes scope has automated its own helplessness.

Sizes measure work content, not elapsed time

An item sized S may sit for three weeks waiting on a partner, a legal review or a shared platform team. That waiting does not appear anywhere in the letters. In most organisations, elapsed time is dominated by queueing, not by effort — which is why teams that halve their estimates see no change in delivery dates. Any forecast built only on effort, with no allowance for dependency wait, is optimistic by construction.

A single number invites padding; a range invites honesty

When an engineer knows a number will be treated as a promise, the rational move is to inflate it, and the inflated estimate then gets consumed by the behaviours Eliyahu Goldratt described — work expanding to fill the time available, and starts deferred until the deadline looms. Ranges break the incentive because they let the engineer be honest about both ends. The organisational precondition is that nobody is punished for the upper bound being high; if they are, the range quietly collapses back into a padded point estimate and you have lost the instrument.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; young company and old

The mechanics are the same everywhere; what changes is which part of the forecast dominates. In a consumer product like Patang's, effort estimates are usually a decent proxy for delivery, because the team controls most of the surface — until an external rail, a payments scheme or an app-store review enters the picture, at which point elapsed time detaches from effort entirely. Consumer teams also under-size the long tail after launch: instrumentation, experiment infrastructure, the second and third iterations that actually produce the outcome. The build is sized; the learning is not.

In B2B and enterprise software the dominant uncertainty is not technical but definitional. "Support customer-specific approval workflows" can be an M or an XL depending on how many of the customers' workflows you promised to support, and that is a commercial question disguised as an engineering one. Mature B2B teams size against a named reference customer's actual configuration rather than against the abstraction. They also carry a category consumer teams rarely do — migration and backward compatibility for existing deployments, which is frequently larger than the feature itself.

Marketplaces add a structural wrinkle: most meaningful features touch two sides plus a trust or operations surface, so items that look like one story are three. A "supplier self-serve pricing" item is a supplier tool, a buyer-side display change, and a fraud-review path. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask, for every item, which sides it touches; anything touching two sides is at least one size larger than it first appears.

Stage matters as much as product type. A twenty-person startup has no history to calibrate against, so its letters convert to nothing, and it should generally forecast by slicing thinly and measuring actual completion over three or four weeks rather than by estimating at all. A thousand-person company has abundant history but an entirely different problem: its items are entangled with other teams, so its forecast error is dominated by cross-team queueing rather than by sizing error. The large company that responds to late delivery by demanding more precise estimates is optimising the term that contributes least.

7. Three common mistakes

Converting sizes to dates with a fixed table

Symptom from outside: a planning document where every L is exactly 15 days and every M exactly 7, and where the total equals capacity almost to the day. Underlying misunderstanding: treating an ordinal scale as a ratio scale, and treating a distribution as a constant. Cheapest diagnostic: ask for the actual durations of the last six items called L. If nobody has them, the conversion is fiction; if they have them and the spread is 19 to 51 days, the single number in the plan is indefensible on its own evidence.

Sizing the solution the PM already has in mind

Symptom: the engineering estimates arrive suspiciously fast and nobody asks a question. Misunderstanding: that the work to be sized is the implementation of a predetermined design, rather than the achievement of an outcome. This forfeits the cheapest source of savings, because engineers who understand the goal routinely propose a different approach one size smaller. Diagnostic: during sizing, ask "if this had to be an S, what would we build instead?" A team that cannot answer has not been told the outcome, only the instruction.

Treating the estimate as the team's promise and the target as the business's due

Symptom: the estimate is debated downward in the meeting itself, and the revised number happens to match the date marketing needs. Misunderstanding: that negotiation changes the work. Diagnostic: compare the last four quarters of "agreed" dates against actual delivery. If the gap is consistent and large, the organisation is not estimating; it is performing a ritual whose output is known in advance, and the engineers have long since stopped putting real information into it.

Reporting only the median

Symptom: status is green for eleven weeks and red in week twelve. Misunderstanding: that the central case is the forecast. Diagnostic: ask what confidence the date carries. If the answer is a blank look, the plan has a 50 percent chance at best, and 50 percent is not a plan when ₹4.2 crore of media is already booked against it.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, this decision is unglamorous. The pod sizes the nine items in forty minutes, silently and independently, and spends most of the time discussing the two items where the spread of opinion was widest. Each item carries one line about what would make it bigger. The PM converts sizes to a range using the team's own last two quarters, states the confidence attached to the date rather than the date alone, and names the single assumption whose failure would move the forecast most. A timeboxed spike is spent buying certainty on that assumption before anyone commits. The forecast is re-run and re-communicated the day the assumption breaks, not the week before launch. And the conversation with the business is about scope and confidence — which two of nine items can go, and what the date is worth at 85 percent instead of 55 — rather than about whether the engineers are sandbagging.

9. What Meera decided

She did not give the CEO a date on 14 April. She gave one on 24 April, after two weeks of buying information, and it came with a number attached to it: all nine items by 30 September at roughly 55 percent confidence, or six of nine items at 85 percent. She proposed the second. Items 7 and 8 — iOS onboarding and the operations reconciliation report — were cut from the launch scope, with iOS users routed to the existing monthly-SIP flow and operations given a nightly export instead of a report. The registrar certification slot was booked on 2 May, eight weeks earlier than the plan required, at the cost of one engineer's time for a fortnight. That was the decision that mattered; the letters only revealed that it mattered.

The reasoning is worth stating in one line, because it generalises past this case: the purpose of a rough size is not to predict the future but to find out, early and cheaply, which uncertainty is worth spending money to remove.

What to learn next follows directly. Capacity planning turns these forecasts into a defensible statement about what a team can hold over a quarter, and it is where the focus factor of 0.55 comes from and can be improved. Prioritising under constraints is the discipline Meera exercised when she cut two of nine items, and it is what makes estimation useful rather than merely accurate. And velocity, throughput and what not to measure matters because the same historical record that makes a forecast honest becomes corrosive the moment it is used to compare teams or to set individual objectives — at which point the numbers stop describing reality and start describing what people want you to believe.

Two questions to sit with.

  1. Your team gives you a size. What would you have to know about the last two quarters before that size could honestly be converted into a date — and if you do not know it, what is the smallest thing you could build in the next three weeks that would tell you more than any further estimation?
  2. Think of a date you have given someone recently. Was it an estimate, a target, a forecast or a commitment — and did the person who heard it understand it as the same one of those four that you meant?

Sources referred to in the text: B. Boehm, Software Engineering Economics (1981); A. Tversky and D. Kahneman, "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases," Science (1974); M. Cohn, Agile Estimating and Planning (2005); S. McConnell, Software Estimation: Demystifying the Black Art (2006). Patang Money and the individuals named are fictional; the market context — UPI Autopay mandates, registrar settlement windows and festive media buying — reflects ordinary Indian practice.

Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing

Rough sizes are cheap to produce and expensive to misuse. This is what separates a practitioner who can run the ritual from one who can referee an argument about it.

1. Two rooms, five weeks apart

On the morning of 11 January 2027, Kavya Deshmukh sat in a glass-walled room on the fourth floor of Trinetra Grid Systems' office in Pune with a sales contract in front of her that she had not written and was about to become responsible for. Trinetra builds meter data management and billing-exception software for electricity distribution utilities — a business of roughly ₹168 crore in annual revenue, 240 people, and an unusually high proportion of customers who are state-owned. The contract was for ₹31.4 crore over three years with a western-state distribution utility, and it carried a clause Kavya had read four times: liquidated damages of 0.5 percent of contract value for every week of delay past a go-live of 1 July 2027, capped at 10 percent.

Twenty-four weeks. The head of sales wanted a signature on a delivery plan by Friday. What Kavya had was a backlog of 84 items that Sudhanshu Rele, her engineering director, had sized over two afternoons — mostly Ms and Ls, four XLs, one item marked simply "unknown, needs a week with their SCADA team." Nothing in that document was a date. Everything in the room wanted to turn it into one.

Five weeks later and 1,100 kilometres away, Rohan Kabra faced a structurally similar problem with almost none of the same raw material. Rohan is Head of Product at Veethika Bazaar, a Jaipur-based marketplace connecting roughly 28,000 handloom and home-furnishing artisans to urban buyers, running about ₹640 crore of annualised gross merchandise value. Veethika's returns experience was, in the board's words on 19 February 2027, "the single largest drag on repeat purchase" — 11.4 percent of orders returned, a median resolution time of 9.2 days, and a seller-satisfaction score that had fallen for three consecutive quarters. The board wanted the overhaul live by 30 June, nineteen weeks away, so that the monsoon quarter could shake it out before the October trading window.

Rohan's difficulty was that his team did not exist in its current form until November 2026. Tanvi Iyengar, his engineering lead, had nine weeks of delivery history, not two years. Every technique that converts sizes into dates by looking backwards had almost nothing to look back at.

These two situations bracket the subject. Kavya has a mature, calibrated team and a fixed scope, a fixed date, and a financial penalty — the case in which estimation is least able to help and is most loudly demanded. Rohan has variable scope and a sympathetic board, which is the case in which estimation could help most, and almost no data with which to do it. The argument of this page is that both of them should stop trying to produce a better number and start trying to produce a better decision about uncertainty — and that the specific moves available to each are different, knowable, and mostly unglamorous.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

Begin with definitions, because most arguments about estimation are arguments about which of four objects is under discussion. An estimate is an unbiased prediction of the quantity of work in an item, produced under uncertainty by people who will do the work. A target is a date the business wants, produced independently of the work. A forecast is a probability distribution over completion dates, produced by combining estimates (or item counts) with observed historical throughput and capacity. A commitment is a promise, and the only defensible basis for one is a forecast at a confidence level the promiser is willing to be judged against. Steve McConnell's formulation in Software Estimation (2006) is the sharpest available: an estimate that has been negotiated downward is no longer an estimate, because the work did not attend the negotiation.

T-shirt sizing — XS, S, M, L, XL — is a deliberately coarse ordinal scale used to size items relative to each other rather than in absolute time. Its immediate ancestors are the story point, introduced within Extreme Programming around 1997–99 by Kent Beck, Ron Jeffries and colleagues, and Planning Poker, invented by James Grenning in 2002 as a defence against a single dominant voice anchoring a group and popularised by Mike Cohn in Agile Estimating and Planning (2005). Behind both stands Barry Boehm's Wideband Delphi from Software Engineering Economics (1981), itself an adaptation of the RAND Corporation's Delphi method: independent estimates, revealed simultaneously, followed by discussion of the reasons for divergence and a second round. Boehm's book also gave the field COCOMO, the first widely used parametric cost model, and — through Steve McConnell's later popularisation — the cone of uncertainty, the empirical observation that early estimates on real projects are distributed roughly between a quarter and four times the eventual actual.

The problem being solved is narrow and real: humans are poor at absolute magnitude judgements on unfamiliar work and reliably optimistic, because the work not yet understood is invisible and therefore weightless in the mental model. Humans are considerably better at ordinal comparison. Relative sizing trades on the faculty that functions.

What follows is where competent practitioners genuinely part company. There are five identifiable schools, and it is worth stating for each the proposition it would sign and the one it would not.

The calibrated-estimation school (Boehm, McConnell, and the Personal Software Process lineage) holds that estimation is a measurable skill that improves with feedback, and that the remedy for bad estimates is recorded actuals and calibration, not abandonment. It would sign: "a team that records actuals against estimates for two quarters will estimate materially better in the third." It would not sign: "a point estimate without a stated range is ever acceptable."

The relative-sizing school (Cohn, Grenning) holds that absolute duration estimates are hopeless but ordinal comparison is reliable, and that velocity — sizes completed per iteration — converts one to the other. It would sign: "the unit of estimation should be dimensionless." It would not sign: "sizes should be converted to hours by a fixed table," which is, ironically, the thing most organisations do in its name.

The probabilistic flow school (Daniel Vacanti, Troy Magennis, and the Kanban tradition) holds that per-item sizes add little once you have ten or more items, because variation in item size washes out against variation in throughput, and that the right instrument is a Monte Carlo simulation over historical weekly throughput. It would sign: "for a backlog of thirty items, counting items forecasts as well as sizing them." It would not sign: "item size never matters" — it matters acutely when the size distribution is fat-tailed.

The #NoEstimates school (Woody Zuill, Vasco Duarte, from around 2012) holds that per-item estimation is waste that produces the illusion of control, and that the discipline should instead be slicing work until items are roughly uniform and small, then shipping and counting. It would sign: "most estimation effort would produce more value if spent slicing." It would not sign: "no forecast is ever required," although it is frequently and unfairly read as saying exactly that.

The reference-class school derives from Kahneman and Tversky's distinction between the inside view and the outside view, and from Bent Flyvbjerg's work on megaproject overruns. It holds that the estimate a team produces by decomposing its own plan is systematically optimistic, and that the only reliable correction is the distribution of outcomes for similar past efforts by anyone. It would sign: "your team's decomposition is less predictive than the record of the last ten projects of this type." It would not sign: "the reference class is easy to choose" — which is its own weakest joint.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

Expert practice has roughly seven moves. Four are commonly taught; three are usually left implicit and are where most of the value sits.

The first move is fixing and maintaining a reference anchor. Relative sizing without a named reference item is absolute estimation wearing a costume. Trinetra's reference M is a specific job from August 2026: "add a new exception rule to the billing-exception engine, with its configuration screen and its audit entry." The implicit part is maintaining it. As a team becomes fluent in a domain, work that was an M becomes an S in felt difficulty, and if the anchor is not periodically re-validated against actuals, the whole scale drifts and the historical conversion silently breaks.

The second move is sizing effort, complexity and uncertainty jointly, and never duration. The third is independent estimation before discussion — the Delphi structure — for the specific reason that the information sits in the disagreement. The fourth is recording, for each item, the assumption whose failure would change the size. "L, assuming the utility exposes meter reads over their existing head-end API" is an estimate you can act on. "L" is a letter.

The fifth move, usually implicit, is splitting anything that lands at XL, on the principle that ordinal judgement degrades beyond roughly one order of magnitude from the anchor. The sixth is applying a split factor: the empirical ratio between the number of items a backlog contains at planning time and the number it contains at completion. At Trinetra, across the last four delivery programmes, that ratio is 1.55. Not applying it is the single most common reason for a plan that was correct item-by-item and wrong in total.

The seventh move is converting to a forecast using the arithmetic of distributions rather than the arithmetic of sums, and it is worth doing slowly because almost everybody gets it wrong in one of two opposite directions.

Take a simplified backlog: twelve items, each with an expected effort of 8 engineer-days and a standard deviation of 5 engineer-days. A manager who wants an 85th-percentile plan typically takes the 85th percentile of each item — about 8 + 1.04 × 5 = 13.2 days — and adds them up: 12 × 13.2 = 158 engineer-days. This is the sum of the percentiles, and it is not the percentile of the sum.

If the items are independent, variances add, so the standard deviation of the total is 5 × √12 = 17.3 days against a mean of 96. The 85th percentile of the total is then 96 + 1.04 × 17.3 = 114 engineer-days. The naive method has overstated the pessimistic case by 39 percent, and a team planned against it will be given 44 more days than the risk warrants, which Parkinson's law will cheerfully absorb.

But independence is a strong assumption and usually false. Suppose the items are correlated with ρ = 0.4 — a realistic figure when seven of twelve items depend on the same external certification, or the same unfamiliar framework, or the same two senior engineers. Then the variance of the sum is σ²(n + n(n−1)ρ) = 25 × (12 + 132 × 0.4) = 25 × 64.8 = 1,620, giving a standard deviation of 40.2 and an 85th percentile of 96 + 41.9 = 138 engineer-days. And at perfect correlation, ρ = 1, the standard deviation is 5 × 12 = 60 and the 85th percentile is exactly 158 — the naive sum.

Adding up the pessimistic case of every item is not conservatism. It is the precise mathematical assumption that everything goes wrong at the same time, for the same reason.

There is a second-order effect that experts watch for and novices do not: the act of estimating changes the thing estimated. Once velocity is reported upward, points inflate — the same work is rated higher next quarter — and the metric detaches from output, which is Goodhart's law arriving on schedule. Once an estimate is treated as a promise, padding becomes rational, and padded estimates are then consumed by Parkinson's law and by what Eliyahu Goldratt called student syndrome: work begun late because the buffer was visible. None of these are failures of character. They are predictable responses to what the organisation does with the number.

4. Conditions, stated as claims you can test

The usefulness of size-based forecasting rests on five conditions. Each can be checked in an afternoon, and each fails differently for Kavya and for Rohan.

Claim one: the team has at least twenty completed, comparable items with recorded sizes and actuals in the last two quarters. Trinetra has 117. Veethika has 41, but all from nine weeks with a team whose composition changed twice. Kavya passes; Rohan fails, and the correct response to failing is not to estimate harder but to switch instruments — to slice thin, measure throughput for three or four weeks, and forecast from counts.

Claim two: the new items are drawn from the same population as the history. This is the claim most often waved through. Trinetra's backlog contains a SCADA integration with a control-system vendor the team has never worked with; that item is not from the same population as 117 billing-engine items, and its size carries no information. The expert move is to segregate such items from the calibrated arithmetic entirely and treat them as timeboxed investigations with explicit decision points.

Claim three: elapsed time is dominated by effort rather than by queueing. Measure flow efficiency — touch time divided by elapsed time. Trinetra's is 31 percent, which is high for enterprise software. Veethika's is 12 percent, because most items wait on a third-party logistics partner's weekly integration window. For Rohan, halving every estimate would change his delivery date by very little; the queue, not the work, owns his calendar.

Claim four: scope is genuinely variable. Estimation is decision-support for scope. Kavya's scope is contractually fixed and her date carries a penalty, which means her estimates cannot inform the decision they are designed to inform. In that regime estimation converts into something else: risk pricing. This is not a degradation — it is a different and entirely legitimate use — but pretending it is planning is how people get hurt.

Claim five: nobody is penalised for a high upper bound. If the organisation punishes pessimism, ranges collapse into padded points within two quarters and the instrument stops carrying information. The diagnostic is simple and rarely run: ask three engineers privately what they would have said if the number were not going into a plan.

There are situations in which sizing is not merely unhelpful but actively misleading. Fixed-scope, fixed-date contracts, where a precise-looking forecast manufactures false comfort. Genuinely novel technical work, where the uncertainty is about feasibility rather than quantity — you cannot size "get this model from 71 percent precision to 90 percent," because nobody knows whether it is a week or impossible. Work dominated by cross-team dependency, where accurate effort estimates produce confidently wrong dates. And very small samples, where the arithmetic has the appearance of statistics without the substance.

5. Hard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

In multi-product companies with shared platforms, the seam is where forecasts die. Two teams each estimate their half competently, each is right, and the joint delivery takes two and a half times the sum, because the handoffs impose queues that neither team's estimate contains. Trinetra's data-platform group in Bengaluru serves four product lines; a two-day change to its ingestion schema has a median wait of eleven days. The mature move is to forecast the seam explicitly as its own item with its own historical wait-time distribution, rather than as an asterisk.

In two-sided marketplaces, a single user-visible change is usually three pieces of work — buyer surface, seller surface, and an operations or trust surface — plus a partner integration. Veethika's first five weeks of slicing revealed a split factor of 1.9, not the 1.4 Tanvi had assumed. The diagnostic is embarrassingly cheap: for every item, ask which sides it touches, and treat anything touching two as at least one size larger than it first appears.

In regulated domains, the build is a minority of the effort. Trinetra's metering work must satisfy state regulatory metering and audit requirements, and the evidence pack — test artefacts, traceability from requirement to test case, sign-off cycles — has historically run at 0.7 times the build effort and, crucially, occurs after it, on a calendar owned by someone else. Teams that size the build and forget the evidence are consistently and predictably late by a proportion that is itself measurable.

In hardware-plus-software, the calendar is owned by lead times. Hirak Devices in Coimbatore, which makes smart water meters with firmware and a cloud back end, takes nine weeks for a printed-circuit-board respin whatever anyone estimates. Software estimates there matter only insofar as they exceed the hardware critical path; below it, further estimation precision buys nothing at all, and the honest planning question is which software work must be finished before the respin is committed.

In AI-native work, the uncertainty is categorically different. Veethika's proposed automatic defect detection on returns photographs cannot be sized, because the quantity of work depends on whether the approach works. What experts do instead is bound the downside: a six-week timebox, a pre-registered kill criterion (precision at or above 0.85 at recall 0.60 on a held-out set of 4,000 labelled returns), and a costed fallback — human review at ₹41 per case across roughly 3,100 cases a month, or ₹1.27 lakh monthly. The forecast is then not about the model but about the decision date, which is knowable.

What mature organisations actually do, as distinct from what their process documents claim, is worth saying plainly. They say they run story points and velocity. What they in fact run is a small number of dated commitments carrying substantial buffers held centrally by a programme manager, a much larger body of undated work that flows, and — this is the part nobody writes down — a private list, usually three or four items long, of the things everyone senior believes will actually slip. Expertise partly consists of knowing that this list exists, asking for it early, and treating it as the real plan.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The outlier estimator holds the information

When one engineer says XL and five say M, the average is worthless and the discussion is everything. Tell-tale sign: an expert facilitator asks the highest estimator to speak first and asks what they can see that the others cannot. The obvious reading — that the outlier is noise to be smoothed — is wrong, because estimates diverge for reasons, and the reason is usually a piece of work the majority has not imagined.

Splitting legitimately increases the total, and that is not scope creep

Decompose an item sized L into six pieces and the pieces frequently sum to more than the L, because decomposition surfaces work that the coarse estimate had absorbed invisibly. Tell-tale sign: a manager accusing the team of gold-plating after a refinement session. The expert reading is the opposite: the increase is the estimate becoming accurate, and the right response is a scope conversation, not a discipline conversation.

The anchor drifts and nobody notices

Tell-tale sign: velocity rising steadily over three quarters with no corresponding rise in shipped outcomes. Either points have inflated or the reference item has silently shrunk. The diagnostic is to re-size four items from a year ago, blind, and compare with what they were called then.

Flow efficiency, not estimation accuracy, usually owns the date

Most teams' touch time is between 5 and 15 percent of elapsed time. Tell-tale sign: estimates that are accurate item-by-item while delivery dates slip anyway. An expert measures the ratio before touching the estimation process, because a team at 10 percent efficiency can double its productivity and move its date by a few days.

The definition of done is where the tail hides

Tell-tale sign: a plan with a "code complete" milestone. Migration, feature flags, monitoring, runbooks, support training, rollback rehearsal and the regulatory evidence pack are all real work, all routinely outside the sized item, and collectively often 40 to 80 percent of it in enterprise settings.

Padding is a measurement of trust, not of the work

Tell-tale sign: the same team giving materially different estimates for comparable work depending on who is in the room. The naive reading is dishonesty; the expert reading is that the estimate now encodes the estimator's forecast of how the number will be used, which is rational and which no amount of training will remove while the usage stays the same.

Ordinal scales cannot be arithmetic without an empirical bridge

Tell-tale sign: a spreadsheet in which L equals exactly two M. Sizes become summable only through this team's observed distribution for each size over a recent window. A conversion table borrowed from a sister team is decoration, and it is the most common proximate cause of large misses.

Estimation's chief product is design, not numbers

Tell-tale sign: during a sizing session, an expert changes the design — "if we let the first release read from the existing nightly file instead of the live API, is this an S?" — and the estimate becomes irrelevant because the work did. Teams that treat sizing as a measurement exercise forfeit the largest available saving, which is always scope and approach rather than accuracy.

The second half is not like the first half

Tell-tale sign: status reported as percent complete rather than as items done and items remaining. Integration, edge cases and defect repair concentrate at the end, so a programme genuinely 50 percent through its items is rarely 50 percent through its calendar. Counting completed items exposes this; percentage estimates conceal it by construction.

7. Where the product type and company stage genuinely change the answer

Some differences are real and some are folklore, and it is worth separating them. In consumer products, effort is usually a decent proxy for delivery because the team controls most of the surface, and the characteristic error is not mis-sizing the build but omitting the post-launch tail: instrumentation, experiment infrastructure, and the two or three iterations that actually produce the outcome. In B2B and enterprise, the dominant uncertainty is definitional rather than technical — "support customer-specific approval workflows" ranges from M to XL depending on a commercial promise, not an engineering fact — and migration and backward compatibility are frequently larger than the feature. In platform work, the consumer of the estimate is another engineering team, which makes the estimate unusually honest and unusually useless, because platform work's value is realised only when downstream teams adopt it and adoption is not on the platform team's backlog.

In marketplaces, as already noted, the multiplier is structural. In hardware, lead times dominate and the software estimate matters only against the critical path. In AI products, the distinction between quantity uncertainty and feasibility uncertainty is the whole game, and treating the second as the first is the field's characteristic error.

Where the difference is not real, and is often claimed: the mechanics of relative sizing do not change by domain. The reference anchor, the independent first round, the assumption note, the split at XL, the empirical conversion — these are the same in a payments company and a diagnostics company, and teams that believe their domain requires a bespoke estimation philosophy are usually avoiding the measurement step.

Stage changes things sharply in one direction. A twenty-person company has no usable history, so its correct method is Rohan's: slice to roughly uniform items, ship, count, and forecast from four weeks of throughput while saying clearly that the sample is thin. A two-thousand-person company has abundant history and a different problem — cross-team queueing dominates its forecast error — so its instinct to demand more precise estimates optimises the term contributing least. The single most common large-company pathology is investing heavily in estimation accuracy while flow efficiency sits at 8 percent.

8. Three worked examples

Trinetra: a fixed date with a financial penalty

Kavya did not try to convert 84 items into a date. She did four things in sequence. First, she applied Trinetra's measured split factor: 84 × 1.55 ≈ 130 items by completion. Second, she segregated the four XLs and the SCADA unknown from the arithmetic and gave each a timeboxed investigation with a decision date. Third, she took the pod's weekly completed-item counts for the previous 26 weeks — median 6.2 items per week, worst eight-week stretch averaging 4.1, best 8.9 — and forecast from counts rather than from sizes.

The simulation put the probability of completing all 130 items within 24 weeks at roughly 58 percent. Kavya's fourth move was to price that rather than argue about it. Liquidated damages run at 0.5 percent of ₹31.4 crore, or ₹15.7 lakh per week. If the probability of being late is 0.42 and the expected lateness given lateness is about 3.4 weeks, the expected penalty is 0.42 × 3.4 × ₹15.7 lakh ≈ ₹22.4 lakh, against a worst case of the 10 percent cap, ₹3.14 crore.

Twenty-two lakh on a ₹31.4 crore contract is a 0.7 percent risk-adjusted cost, which is a smaller number than anyone in the room had been arguing about for a fortnight. That reframing let Kavya make the argument she actually wanted to make: the risk was worth carrying, but it should be reduced by structure rather than by optimism. She negotiated a phased go-live — the billing-exception module bearing the penalty on 1 July, meter-data ingestion on 1 October — which moved 38 items out of the penalised milestone and took the probability of on-time delivery of the penalised scope from 58 percent to roughly 88 percent.

Kanchan Insure Systems: where the approach failed

Kanchan Insure Systems, a Hyderabad firm building health-claims adjudication software for third-party administrators, ran a 26-week programme in 2025 that took 55 weeks — an overrun of 112 percent — despite doing everything the textbook asks. Items were sized in T-shirts by the engineers doing the work, independently, with a second Delphi round. The sizes themselves were, in the post-mortem, accurate: comparing recorded touch time with sizes, the ordering held and the medians were close.

Two things went wrong, and neither was estimation quality. First, sizes were converted to dates using a table borrowed from a sister team — L equals 15 engineer-days — that had never been validated against Kanchan's own actuals; their own L had a median of 21 days and an 80th percentile of 44. Second, and larger, 71 percent of elapsed time was queueing on a shared identity-and-consent platform team. Measured after the fact, flow efficiency was 7 percent: a median item carried nine days of touch time inside 128 days of elapsed time.

The recovery is instructive because it contained almost no estimation work. Kanchan built its own thin implementation of the three identity endpoints it actually needed, removing the shared-team dependency for that programme. Flow efficiency rose from 7 percent to 22 percent within a quarter. The team stopped converting sizes by table and began forecasting from its own weekly throughput with a Monte Carlo simulation. On the next release, the 85th-percentile forecast was 14 weeks and delivery took 16 — an error of 14 percent against the previous 112. The estimates had not improved. The system had.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs and the cost of late detection

Table-based conversion of sizes to days. Early sign: a plan in which the totals land suspiciously close to available capacity. Diagnostic question: what were the actual durations of the last six items you called L? Caught early, it costs an afternoon of data extraction; caught late, it costs the whole variance of the programme, as at Kanchan.

Ignoring the split factor. Early sign: the backlog grows during delivery and each addition is justified individually, so nobody totals them. Diagnostic: at week four, compare current item count to the planning count and extrapolate. Caught at week four the response is a scope decision; caught at week sixteen it is a crisis meeting.

Reporting the median as the plan. Early sign: status green for eleven weeks, red in week twelve. Diagnostic: what confidence does this date carry? Cost of catching late is not the delay itself but the loss of every cheaper option that existed while there was still time to descope.

Estimating the build and not the release. Early sign: a milestone called "code complete." Diagnostic: walk one representative item through to a user actually using it in production and list everything that happened. Caught late, it produces the familiar and demoralising pattern of a team that is "done" for six weeks before anything ships.

Velocity as a performance measure. Early sign: points per sprint rising while shipped outcomes do not. Diagnostic: count items and outcomes, not points, for one quarter. The cost of catching this late is the permanent loss of the instrument — once velocity is a performance metric, no future estimate from that team carries information.

Treating feasibility uncertainty as quantity uncertainty. Early sign: a research item with a size on it. Diagnostic: ask what result would make us stop. If there is no answer, it is not a sized item; it is an open-ended bet, and it should be bounded by time and by a stated kill criterion.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether per-item estimation earns its keep at all. The flow-forecasting and #NoEstimates positions rest on real evidence: for backlogs above roughly ten items, Monte Carlo simulations driven purely by item counts and historical throughput forecast about as well as simulations that incorporate per-item sizes, because item-size variation is small relative to throughput variation. The calibrated-estimation position rests on equally real evidence: teams that record actuals against estimates measurably improve, and organisations that must price fixed-scope contracts have no alternative instrument. What would have to be true for the flow position to be wrong is that item size distributions are fat-tailed enough for a single monster to dominate the total — which is exactly the case in platform migrations and regulated integrations. What would have to be true for the calibration position to be wrong is that the estimating effort displaces slicing effort of greater value, which is frequently observed and rarely measured.

Dimensionless points versus honest days. The relative-sizing school argues that dimensionless units resist conversion into commitments. The opposing view, held by many experienced engineering leaders, is that points are a euphemism that fools nobody — everyone in the building silently divides by velocity — and that estimating in ideal engineer-days is at least legible, auditable and comparable to actuals. The strongest version of the points argument is not about accuracy but about politics: a dimensionless unit is harder to weaponise. The strongest version of the days argument is that obscuring the unit has not, in practice, prevented weaponisation and has made calibration harder.

The inside view versus the outside view. Reference-class forecasting says your decomposition is systematically optimistic and the record of similar past efforts is more predictive. Its weakness is the selection of the class: "similar" is doing enormous work, and a team can honestly select a reference class that produces any answer it likes. Practitioners who reject it are usually rejecting not the logic but the availability of a defensible class in software, where "similar project" is much slipperier than in bridge-building.

Explicit buffers versus probabilistic forecasts. Critical-chain practice pools safety into a visible project buffer and manages its consumption. Probabilistic practice refuses buffers and reports a distribution instead. The buffer camp argues that executives need a single date and that the honest version of a single date is a date plus a managed buffer. The distribution camp argues that any single date, however buffered, will be treated as a commitment and that the discipline of stating confidence is precisely what teaches an organisation to think about risk. Both are correct about the failure mode they fear, and there is no synthesis that both would sign.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces better artefacts: cleaner backlogs, tidier sizes, a range instead of a point. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They ask what the estimate is for before producing one, and they decline to produce one when the answer is "so we can hold the team to it" without also renegotiating what holding means. They spend their scarce influence on the correlation structure rather than on individual accuracy — decoupling from the shared dependency, splitting the monster item, buying the certification slot early — because that is where the tail lives. They measure the boring quantities nobody asks for: split factor, flow efficiency, the spread inside each size band, the gap between "code complete" and "in production." And they treat the sizing session as a design review, changing the work when the size is unacceptable rather than changing the number.

There is a fifth, subtler mark. Experts are comfortable saying, in front of senior people, "the honest answer is that we do not know yet, here is what it will cost to know, and here is the date by which I will tell you." That sentence is not evasion; it is a commitment with a shorter horizon and a higher probability, and organisations learn to trust it faster than they learn to trust dates.

12. What each of them decided

Kavya signed the delivery plan, but not the one sales had drafted. She proposed a phased go-live that moved 38 items out of the penalty-bearing milestone, took the probability of on-time delivery of that milestone from 58 to roughly 88 percent, and priced the residual risk at about ₹22 lakh expected — a figure she put in the contract review memo so that the commercial team was carrying an assessed risk rather than an assumed certainty. She also spent one engineer for two weeks on the SCADA investigation before the plan was signed, on the grounds that the single unknown item carried more variance than the other 83 combined.

Rohan committed to scope rather than to a date, published a two-weekly forecast with confidence attached, and put the defect-detection model behind a six-week timebox with a stated kill criterion and a costed human fallback. He also did the least glamorous thing on the list: he asked Tanvi to measure flow efficiency, discovered it was 12 percent, and moved the logistics partner's integration window from weekly to twice weekly — a change that shortened his forecast by more than any conceivable improvement in estimation would have.

Discussion questions.

  1. Kavya's contract fixes both scope and date and attaches a penalty. In that regime, what is estimation actually for — and what would you have told the head of sales in the week before the clause was agreed, when the estimate could still have changed something?
  2. Rohan has nine weeks of history and a board that wants a date. Is a forecast built on such a thin sample better or worse than no forecast at all, and what obligation does he have to communicate the width of the uncertainty rather than its centre?
  3. Kanchan's estimates were accurate and its programme overran by 112 percent. If you were the incoming VP of Engineering, in what order would you attack split factor, flow efficiency, conversion method and definition of done — and what evidence would justify that order?

13. Going deeper

Agile in practice is the immediate predecessor: estimation is the mechanism by which iterative teams size work, and understanding the iteration rhythm explains why sizes are refreshed rather than fixed. Prioritising under constraints is what makes estimation useful at all — a size that never changes a scope decision has cost more than it returned. Capacity planning supplies the other half of every forecast, including the focus factor that turns headcount into available engineer-days and is usually far lower than managers assume. Velocity, throughput and what not to measure is the essential corrective: the same historical record that makes forecasting honest becomes corrosive the moment it is used to compare teams. The software development lifecycle explains why the work after "code complete" is real work and where it sits. Kanban and flow supplies Little's Law, flow efficiency and the Monte Carlo machinery that outperforms sizing in most modern settings. The execution rhythm determines how often a forecast is refreshed and therefore how quickly bad news travels. Backlog management and refinement is where the split factor is created or controlled, and where sizing sessions do their real work as design reviews. Definition of done is the single cheapest intervention on forecast accuracy, because it determines what the size was a size of. And the PM–engineering relationship underwrites all of it: none of these techniques survive in an organisation where an honest upper bound is punished.

Ashtapada Systems: Three Dates and One Board Meeting

A teaching case on rough sizes, hard commitments, and a portfolio plan that no longer adds up.

1. Sunday night in Aundh

At 10.20 pm on Sunday, 27 September 2026, Devika Iyer sat at the dining table of her flat in Aundh, Pune, with a fourteen-slide deck open in front of her and slide nine still blank. The slide was titled "FY27 Delivery Commitments", and it was the only slide the board's product and technology sub-committee would actually argue about when it met at 9.30 am on Monday.

Devika had been Chief Product Officer of Ashtapada Systems for nineteen months. In January the board had approved a plan with three dated commitments on it, and until three weeks ago she had believed all three would land. Now her VP of Engineering was telling her that at most two would, her Chief Revenue Officer had already told a client in Dubai that the most fragile of the three would be early, and the engineering leader who had proposed the whole sizing system in the first place wanted to abolish it before Monday. The rain had started again outside. Devika had until roughly seven o'clock the next morning to decide what went on slide nine, and whether the number on it was a date, a range, or an apology.

2. Ashtapada Systems

Ashtapada Systems was founded in Pune in 2017 by Aniruddh Bhonsle and two colleagues who had spent a decade building core-banking integrations for Indian lenders. Its product, Paasa, was a loan-origination and co-lending platform: it took a borrower application from an NBFC's app or a partner's storefront, ran the bureau and income checks, split the loan between the NBFC and its partner bank according to the agreed ratio, pushed the disbursal instruction, and then kept the two lenders' books reconciled for the life of the loan. By September 2026 the company had 310 employees, 118 of them in engineering, and ₹64 crore of annual recurring revenue from 41 lenders.

One earlier decision shaped everything about the present one. In March 2025, Ashtapada acquired a nine-person collections-analytics team in Bengaluru for ₹11 crore in cash and stock. The acquisition was a good one: the team's repayment-propensity models became Paasa's most-demoed feature within a year. But two promises were made at signing, and both were made by Aniruddh personally. The first was that the Bengaluru team would keep its own way of working — it did not use story points, it measured cycle time and throughput, and its lead had made this a condition of joining. The second was that within two years the two codebases would be merged into a single platform, internally called Paasa 3.0, because the company could not sell an integrated product off two separate ledgers forever. Eighteen months later, the company was running two estimation cultures inside one portfolio plan, and the merge had not started.

3. The industry

Indian digital lending in 2026 was a market of infrastructure providers sitting between regulated entities. Ashtapada competed against Lentra, Perfios and Yubi for origination and co-lending mandates, and against the in-house platform teams that the larger NBFCs had begun to build. It sat on rails it did not own: the Account Aggregator framework for consented financial data, NPCI's UPI and NACH mandates for collection, CKYC for identity, and the credit bureaus for risk. Its customers were the institutions that used those rails — the NBFCs, small finance banks and private banks whose co-lending books had grown through the decade.

Two regulatory currents mattered. The Reserve Bank of India's co-lending directions had tightened what a platform must prove about how a loan is split, escrowed and reported, and auditors had begun asking lenders for instrument-level rather than portfolio-level evidence. Separately, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had turned data-handling into a board question. The RBI's earlier tightening of risk weights on unsecured consumer credit had slowed Ashtapada's NBFC customers, which is why the company had gone looking for growth abroad.

That search led to the Gulf. In November 2025, Ashtapada signed Al Hisn Finance, a Dubai consumer lender, on a three-year contract worth ₹18 crore, its largest ever. The Gulf was attractive for the usual reasons — proximity, a large Indian diaspora among the end customers, and no local equivalent of Paasa. It was hard for reasons Pune had underestimated: data-residency expectations, an Arabic-first interface, a different working week, and a client whose year revolved around Ramadan.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

On 3 and 4 February 2026, twenty-two engineers and product managers spent two days sizing the FY27 portfolio. They used the T-shirt ladder in Exhibit 1, which Aniruddh had written in 2021 for a single Pune team of eleven people and which had not been revised since. Seven initiatives were sized. The resulting commitment sheet, Exhibit 2, went to the board on 19 February and was approved with what the minutes called "a fifteen per cent buffer".

Three of the seven initiatives carried external dates. The co-lending compliance module, which would produce instrument-level split, escrow and audit reporting for partner banks, was committed for 31 March 2027, because that was when the first partner bank's internal audit cycle closed. The Al Hisn go-live in Dubai was committed for 1 February 2027. Paasa 3.0, the platform merge, was committed to begin in Q3 FY27 and complete within FY28.

At the time, four things were believed. First, that the sizes from the two pods were comparable, because both had used the same ladder in the same room. Second, that the compliance module was an M, because the Pune pod owned the ledger and the sizing convention was to record the owning pod's number — the Bengaluru pod had said XL, and the XL was noted in a comment thread but not on the sheet. Third, that engineering had 118 people, of whom 96 were available for portfolio work. Fourth, that the Al Hisn build was mostly configuration, since the lending flows were the same ones Paasa already ran in India.

By September, all four had come apart. In April the Bengaluru pod, under pressure to report on the same dashboard as everyone else, re-baselined its story points to the Pune scale. Its measured velocity rose from the low twenties to the low forties over the next four sprints, which is what Exhibit 4 shows, and which nobody in the finance or board packs read as anything other than a team getting faster. Nobody re-sized the portfolio after the re-baselining, so Exhibit 2 still carries February's numbers on a scale that stopped existing in April.

In August, the partner bank's auditors told the bank — and the bank told Ashtapada — that the instrument-level evidence they wanted had to include a restatement of fourteen months of existing book, with dual-control approvals on every reconciliation adjustment. That was not in anyone's February picture. The Bengaluru pod, which had said XL in February, now said the restatement alone was an XL and the forward-looking module was a second XL.

On 8 September, Priyanka Nair's risk data-science group in Toronto reported that the repayment-propensity models could not be retrained for the UAE portfolio on Indian infrastructure, because Al Hisn's counsel had advised the client that borrower data should remain within the UAE. A separate training environment inside a UAE region, with its own deployment pipeline and its own access controls under the DPDP Act's cross-border obligations on the Indian side, had never been sized at all. It was not on Exhibit 2 because in February it did not exist.

On 18 September, Rohit Dhingra, Chief Revenue Officer, told Al Hisn's chief executive on a call from New Jersey that Ashtapada would be "live before Ramadan", which in 2027 begins in the second week of February. He did not say 1 February and he did not have a size in front of him. Al Hisn's team took it as confirmation and began planning a branch-staff training programme for the last week of January.

On 22 September, Aniruddh circulated a one-page note saying that on current staffing, two of the three dated commitments could land and the third could not, and that he was not yet able to say which two. On 25 September, Shalini Karmarkar, who had come with the Bengaluru acquisition and now ran two of the four pods, sent Devika a throughput-based forecast: on the last fifty completed work items, the compliance module would finish somewhere between eleven and twenty-nine weeks at eighty-five per cent confidence. She attached a note arguing that Ashtapada should stop T-shirt sizing entirely, since the sizes had never predicted anything and now actively misled. Nandita Rao, the CFO, replied within the hour that a range eighteen weeks wide was not something she could put in front of a board or a bank.

5. The people

Devika Iyer — Chief Product Officer, Pune
Position: the portfolio must be re-committed honestly on Monday, in one pass, rather than slipping a date a month at a time. Incentive: her first full FY plan; the board recruited her to bring predictability. Not saying: she signed off the February sheet knowing the compliance module carried two different sizes, and she chose the smaller one because the larger one would have forced a conversation about Paasa 3.0 that she was not ready to have.
Aniruddh Bhonsle — co-founder and VP Engineering, Pune
Position: the sizes were always rough, everyone was told they were rough, and the problem is that the business turned them into dates. Incentive: he wrote the ladder in Exhibit 1 and the acquisition promises in 2025; both are his. Not saying: he believes the Bengaluru pod's XL was right in February and he overruled it to keep the plan fitting, and he has not told Devika that the two engineers who understand the escrow ledger are the same two engineers Paasa 3.0 needs first.
Shalini Karmarkar — Director of Engineering, Bengaluru
Position: abolish sizing; forecast from throughput; commit to ranges and re-forecast fortnightly. Incentive: her team's ESOP tranche vests in March 2027 and she has been asked twice this year to make her people work the way Pune works. Not saying: her own forecast is built on fifty items from collections analytics, work with almost nothing in common with escrow reconciliation, and she knows the sample does not transfer.
Rohit Dhingra — Chief Revenue Officer, New Jersey
Position: Al Hisn is untouchable; it is the reference account for four more Gulf deals in the pipeline worth ₹40 crore. Incentive: his variable pay is weighted to new-logo ARR in the Gulf and North America. Not saying: he has already pencilled two of those four deals into the FY27 forecast Nandita gave the board, on the assumption that Al Hisn goes live in February and can be cited by March.
Nandita Rao — Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai
Position: whatever is decided, she needs single dates she can use in revenue recognition and in a conversation with the lender behind the ₹25 crore venture-debt facility. Incentive: the facility's covenant is tested on FY27 ARR. Not saying: she has run the numbers on a February slip and knows the covenant survives it; she has not shared this because she would rather the delivery conversation not be conducted around the floor she can tolerate.
Priyanka Nair — Head of Risk Data Science, Toronto
Position: the UAE training environment is at least twelve weeks of work that is on nobody's plan, and shipping Al Hisn without retrained models means shipping Indian repayment behaviour into a Gulf book. Incentive: model quality is what she is measured on; a bad Gulf book would be attributed to her group. Not saying: a simpler rules-based fallback would probably hold for two quarters, and she has not offered it because she does not want it to become permanent.
Lena Vogt — Principal Designer, Berlin
Position: the Arabic right-to-left interface is not a translation task; it touches ninety-one screens. Incentive: she has argued for two years that design work is invisible in the sizing ladder. Not saying: she has already built a working RTL prototype in her own time, which would shorten the work considerably, and she is holding it back until design is written into the estimate properly.
Serene Goh — Director of Customer Success, APAC & MEA, Singapore
Position: tell Al Hisn now, in September, that the date is moving; do not let branch training be scheduled against a date that will not hold. Incentive: she owns renewal and she will be on the calls in January either way. Not saying: Al Hisn's operations head has already asked her, informally, whether a March date would be workable, and she has not passed that on because Rohit told her not to negotiate scope from Singapore.

7. Voices

"Every one of those sizes had a caveat attached to it in February. Nobody carried the caveats forward. We wrote M on a card in a room; six weeks later it was a date in a board pack with my name against it."
