8. The options as Devika sees them

A. Hold all three dates and buy capacity

Bring in eight contractors from mid-October at ₹1.95 lakh per engineer-week, roughly ₹1.25 crore through March, and hold February for Al Hisn, March for compliance and a Q3 start for Paasa 3.0. Exhibit 4 can be read as supporting this: capacity is rising. Exhibit 6 makes the money look affordable against ₹18 crore and a ₹40 crore pipeline. What this reading does not carry is the footnote about ramp time, or that contractors cannot be put on the escrow ledger, which is where the scarce knowledge sits.

B. Protect compliance, move the Gulf to May

Treat the partner-bank audit as the one immovable commitment, because ₹22 crore of ARR sits behind contracts that permit exit on unremedied regulatory non-conformance, and tell Al Hisn this week that go-live moves to May. This costs up to ₹36 lakh in penalties, the ₹1.6 crore milestone slips a quarter, and Rohit's two forecast Gulf deals lose their reference. It also assumes the compliance module is genuinely an XL-plus-XL rather than an M, which is precisely the thing nobody has re-sized.

C. Split the Gulf launch

Go live in Dubai on 1 February with rules-based risk rather than retrained models, English-first with Arabic on the highest-traffic twenty screens, and a manual reconciliation process for the first quarter. Priyanka has not put this on the table, and Lena's unused prototype would make it cheaper than anyone has costed. The risk is that a thin launch becomes the permanent product, and that Serene's team absorbs three months of manual work for a client that was sold something else.

D. Change the instrument, not the plan

Take Shalini's position: stop recording T-shirt sizes on the commitment sheet, publish ranges with confidence levels, and re-forecast every fortnight. This is the most honest description of what Ashtapada actually knows. It is also the hardest thing to say to a sub-committee that has asked for one slide, to a CFO with a covenant, and to a client whose branch training is already scheduled; and Shalini's fifty-item sample comes from collections analytics, not from escrow reconciliation.

Devika had written the four options out twice, and both times the same thought had interrupted her: that the options were all answers to the question "what date do we give", and that the question might instead be which of the three commitments should have been on the sheet at all. Paasa 3.0 had no external customer waiting for it and no penalty attached, and Aniruddh's note had been carefully silent about whether it was one of the two that could land. Nobody had asked, in February or since, what would happen if the merge simply did not start this year.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The sub-committee meets at 9.30 am on Monday, 28 September, the full board on 9 October, and Nandita's lender review on 16 October. A hiring freeze on permanent engineering roles has held since June, lifted only for backfills. The compliance date is set by a partner bank's audit calendar, and three contracts carry exit rights on unremedied regulatory non-conformance. Al Hisn's penalty runs at ₹9 lakh a month, capped at four, with an exclusion whose applicability to the data-residency question is disputed internally. The UAE training environment must sit inside the country, and the Indian side of the transfer must satisfy the DPDP Act. The Bengaluru ESOP tranche vests in March 2027, and Shalini has two engineers holding offers. Lena is the only designer who has worked on the Gulf product and is on leave for the first two weeks of November. Diwali falls in early November, when the Pune office historically loses close to two working weeks.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, did the "M" recorded against the compliance module in Exhibit 2 assert, and what would have had to be true for that assertion to survive until September?
  2. Exhibit 4 shows the Bengaluru pod's output nearly doubling, while Exhibit 3 shows its items taking longer than Pune's at the same recorded size. Reconcile the two. Which of them, if either, should inform Monday's commitment?
  3. The capacity line in Exhibit 2 is 207 points against 180 committed. Work through how that number was built and decide whether the fifteen per cent buffer the board was shown ever existed.
  4. Several people are holding something back: Lena's prototype, Priyanka's fallback, Nandita's covenant headroom, Serene's conversation with the client's operations head. For each, identify what incentive makes silence rational, and what a different planning process would have to do to make disclosure rational instead.
  5. Shalini argues the sizes never predicted anything and should be abandoned. Aniruddh argues the sizes were never meant to predict anything and were misused. Both cannot be fully right. What would you need to observe at Ashtapada over the next quarter to tell which diagnosis is correct?
  6. It is 7 am on Monday. Slide nine is still blank. What do you put on it, what do you tell Rohit to say to Dubai, and how do you answer the sub-committee chair when she asks why the February plan was wrong and why this one is any better?

Sunday, 11.50 pm

Devika made tea she did not drink. On one screen was Shalini's forecast, eleven to twenty-nine weeks, honest and unusable. On another was Rohit's message from New Jersey, sent forty minutes ago, asking only whether February was safe, because Al Hisn's chief executive had asked him the same question that afternoon in Dubai and he had not yet replied. Somewhere in Toronto, Priyanka's evening was still going; the twenty-six-minute window in Exhibit 5 had closed at seven.

She reopened the February sizing document and found the comment thread, four replies long, where the Bengaluru pod had written XL against the compliance module and then let it go. The thread had eleven views. Two of them, she saw, were hers.

Outside, the rain had settled into the steady kind that lasts until morning. Slide nine was still blank.

Himroo Labs: The Al Fareed Date

A teaching case on rough estimates, firm dates, and who is responsible for the gap between them.

1. The decision

It was 7.40 pm on Wednesday, 16 September 2026, and Ananya Rao, Vice President of Product at Himroo Labs, was still at her desk on the fourth floor of the company's office in Bengaluru's Indiranagar, looking at a message from her Head of Engineering that had arrived twenty minutes earlier. Karthik Subramaniam, writing from Pune, had confirmed what his team had suspected for a week: the automated markdown-and-replenishment feature promised to Himroo's largest prospective customer, the Dubai-based hypermarket chain Al Fareed Hypermarkets, could not be built to the date that Sales had already given the client's board. Al Fareed's board was scheduled to approve the three-year contract on Monday, 21 September. Ananya had until 5 pm Friday, 18 September, to tell her Global VP Sales, Rohan Mehta, in New Jersey, what she wanted him to say on his Friday-morning call with Dubai.

2. Himroo Labs

Founded in 2018 by two engineers out of IIT Bombay, Himroo Labs built Loom, a shelf-to-warehouse inventory intelligence platform that told organised retail chains and quick-commerce dark stores what to reorder, when to mark down, and which store clusters were about to run out of stock. The company had grown to roughly 220 employees, 70 of them in engineering, split across Bengaluru and Pune, and reported ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue from 64 paying customers, including regional chains such as Spencer's Retail and Metro Cash & Carry India. It competed for enterprise deals against Increff and Bizom, two established Indian retail-technology firms, and increasingly against the in-house data-science teams that large chains such as Reliance Retail and Trent were building themselves. Through 2025 the company had begun selling into the Gulf, where organised retail was expanding fast and few local vendors offered anything comparable to Loom.

3. The situation

Al Fareed Hypermarkets ran twelve stores across the UAE and was preparing to enter Saudi Arabia. Its board had shortlisted Loom over two competitors, on the condition that Himroo build automated markdown alerts for perishables, a feature no existing customer had asked for in this form. On 25 August, Karthik's pod, four engineers in Bengaluru and two in Pune, had run a T-shirt sizing session on the request and called it an "L": twenty-one to thirty-four story points, an elapsed build time of eight to fourteen weeks, and a note in the sizing doc that the estimate assumed Al Fareed's point-of-sale system exposed a standard live data feed. Karthik had told Rohan directly, in writing, that the size was directional and depended on that assumption holding.

Rohan, needing a date to keep the deal moving, had told Al Fareed's board on 2 September that Loom would go live on 15 January 2027, built from a kickoff on 1 November. He did not check back with Karthik before doing so. Over the following two weeks, Himroo's integration engineers, working with sample exports Al Fareed's IT team sent from Dubai, found that the chain's point-of-sale system, a legacy platform its regional vendor had not updated since 2019, only produced overnight batch files, not a live feed. Building a reliable connector around that gap changed the shape of the work. On 16 September, Karthik resized the feature as an "XL": forty to fifty-five points, sixteen to twenty weeks, implying a go-live near 2 March 2027, roughly seven weeks later than what Al Fareed's board expected to approve on Monday. From Pune, where the discovery work had run late into engineers' evenings after they had already booked leave around Ganesh Chaturthi, Karthik was clear that this number, unlike the first one, was grounded in an actual data sample rather than an assumption.

4. The people

Ananya Rao — Vice President of Product, Bengaluru
Owns the roadmap and the relationship between what engineering can build and what sales sells. Must decide, by Friday, what number to defend.
Karthik Subramaniam — Head of Engineering, Pune
Ran both sizing sessions. Wants the second number, the XL, treated as the real one, and does not want his team's overnight discovery work read as a broken promise.
Rohan Mehta — Global VP Sales, New Jersey
Closed the largest deal of Himroo's history on the strength of the January date. Nine and a half hours behind Bengaluru, he needs an answer before his Friday-morning call with Dubai.
Farah Haddad — Director of Customer Success, APAC & MEA, Singapore
Will own the Al Fareed account after signature and has to live with whatever Ananya promises this week. Wants the client told the truth early rather than discovering a slip in January.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

A. Hold the 15 January date

Ananya tells Rohan to keep the original date and pushes Karthik's pod to compress the build, adding contract engineers over Diwali at an estimated ₹14 lakh. This avoids the penalty clause and any awkward conversation with the board on Monday. Its cost is that the team would be building the connector against a vendor feed it has not fully tested, on a compressed timeline, for the account Himroo can least afford to get wrong; a rushed, buggy launch on Al Fareed's first live weekend would cost more credibility than a delayed one.

B. Renegotiate to 2 March, openly

Ananya asks Rohan to tell Al Fareed's board, before Monday's vote, that discovery uncovered a POS integration Himroo had not priced in, and to offer a concession, such as waiving the first six weeks of fees (≈₹15 lakh), in exchange for the later date. This keeps the estimate honest and protects the engineering team, at the cost of a quarter's revenue recognition and the risk that the board reopens the shortlist to Increff or Bizom before Monday.

C. Split the release

Ananya asks Karthik whether a smaller "M"-sized scope, manual markdown alerts rather than automated ones, can go live on 15 January as promised, with the full automated version following by 2 March. This meets the letter of the original date and buys the extra sixteen weeks honestly, at the cost of roughly ₹12 lakh of interim build that will be discarded in March, two releases for Farah's team to support, and a real risk that Al Fareed's board sees the January release as short of what it was sold.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly did the "L" that Karthik's team gave on 25 August represent, and at what point did it stop being valid?
  2. Where, precisely, did a rough size turn into a client-facing commitment, and whose job was it to stop that from happening without a check-back?
  3. Weigh Ananya's three options against three costs: the cost of a late date, the cost of a broken promise, and the cost the engineering team absorbs in each case.
  4. What should change in how Himroo Labs moves a T-shirt size from an engineering sizing session into a sales conversation, so this gap does not open again?

8. A note for the learner

T-shirt sizing exists to let a team make relative, low-cost planning bets before it has invested in the estimation precision that a real commitment requires. An "L" is a statement about relative complexity and a rough band of elapsed time, conditioned on assumptions that were true at the time it was given, not a promise about a calendar date. The habit that keeps this useful is simple to state and easy to skip under deadline pressure: a rough size can move a roadmap; a hard external date requires that the size be re-confirmed once the assumptions behind it have actually been tested, not merely quoted once and defended forever.

Read this way, the case has a single failure point: Rohan converted a medium-confidence "L", explicitly caveated as depending on an untested POS assumption, into a firm date without looping back to Karthik. That is not a sales failure alone; it is a process gap that Ananya, as the person who owns how estimates travel between engineering and revenue, is responsible for closing. The genuinely difficult part of the decision is not whether the date should move, it clearly should, but how to move it without either burning out the engineering team to save face (Option A) or quietly building throwaway scope to avoid an uncomfortable conversation (Option C).

The most defensible path is Option B: go back to Al Fareed's board before Monday's vote with the real date and the real reason, paired with a concrete goodwill gesture. This is defensible because it treats the estimate for what it always was, a planning input that updates when better information arrives, rather than a number to be protected at any cost once it has been said aloud. It also matches what Farah's team, who must service this account for three years, needs the relationship to be built on. A board that walks away from a vendor for disclosing a real integration finding before signature, rather than after go-live, was unlikely to have been a durable customer in the first place. The lasting fix is procedural, not personal: no T-shirt size crosses from an engineering sizing document into an external date without the engineer who sized it confirming, in writing, that the assumptions still hold.
